# How do I stop “analyzing” and pick between two good choices?
May 8, 2012
•Jason
•Mailbag

*This is part of an ongoing startup advice series where I answer (anonymized!) questions from readers, like a written version ofSmart Bear Live.**To get your question answered**, email me at*`asmartbear -at- shortmail -dot- com`.
Embarras de Choix writes:
> I have a startup with thirty paying customers. We’ve been bootstrapping up to this point.
> > I think there’s a big opportunity to raise money, but also I could continue as I have been. I don’t know way to go.
> > I already know the pros and cons of the decision, so don’t lecture me about that. I just don’t know how to pick!
This is one of those few dilemmas where there’s no wrong answer. So, whichever you choose, never let anyone else make you feel guilty about not choosing the other.
But “there’s no wrong answer” doesn’t answer the question.
Asking for more advice from other people probably won’t resolve it. While I was bootstrappingWP EngineI constantly heard that we’re hamstrung by not taking an investment; after raising a Series A a different set of people expressed their disappointment that I had “sold out.”
Who’s right? Both. Neither. This is why you cannot look externally for the answer.

# A founder asked for my help with a decision last week. · 2026-08-26T00:00:00+00:00

A founder asked for my help with a decision last week.

He runs an agency, and he's spent a while trying to grow a software product on the side. He's finally accepted he can't do both. He wanted help picking one.

He'd clearly done a lot of thinking. Bigger market on the software side, better margins, more scalable. All logical. That was also exactly why he was stuck.

So I asked him one question. If you knew for a fact that both could hit 7 figures a year, which one would you jump out of bed to work on for the next 5 years?

His head still has a job to do here. It has to tell him whether he can realistically get the business where it needs to go. If he can, it's a real option.

But once you've got 2 real options, the spreadsheet can't choose between them. Only you can.

That's the trap: you keep running the numbers, waiting for the logic to make the call, and it never does. So you stay stuck, or you pick whatever looks smartest on paper.

I've done this myself. You choose the thing the spreadsheet says is smart, and 3 years in you can't stand the work. Do you really want to give 10 years of your life to something you have to drag yourself to, just because the market was bigger?

Use your head to work out what's possible. Then let your gut pick the one you actually want to live with for the next 10 years.

# When everything feels equally valid, how do you actually decide?

by Jenny 

I’ve been noticing a pattern in how I (and some founders I’ve been speaking to) get stuck.

It’s not really about lack of information. Or tools. If anything, there’s too much of it.

Different directions, different options and most of them are…reasonable.

That’s where it gets tricky.

Because it’s not obvious what to cut or what to choose.

And the decision isn’t just operational it has high trade-offs and real consequences: direction, positioning, hiring, time, identity even.

A lot of advice focuses on: → prioritisation → metrics → frameworks → tools

And that works…but only once the direction is clear and constraint is identified.

What I’ve been finding is that before that point, those things don’t always help. Sometimes they make it worse.

You can justify almost any path if you frame it the right way.

So you end up looping: reframing, second-guessing, revisiting the same decision again and again (oh, I've been there).

What’s been more useful (at least for me) is slowing down and looking at the decision differently:

→ what does this actually commit me to? → what am I choosing against by picking this? → what becomes harder or impossible if I go this way?

Not just “what sounds good” but what the decision does.

Still figuring this out in practice.
